description: I’m Qaisar Khan, a space-electronics engineer (ex-Sub Engineer, SUPARCO; 2nd place, International CanSat 2024) and CS/Data Science student in Hungary. Team AstroVitals PAK is building a clickable-body astronaut health tool that compares each astronaut with their own baseline, using AI-assisted development. We need a UI/UX designer, a biology/health person, a presenter and a Python/JS developer. Join us to build a focused, demo-ready product in 48 hours.
summary:
AstroVitals PAK is an astronaut health-monitoring and mission-awareness prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It explores how crew self-assessments, simulated health telemetry, descriptive analytics, and mission-related health information can be organized in a unified interface for long-duration spaceflight scenarios.

The platform provides a four-member synthetic crew dashboard, manual health check-ins, historical health trends, an interactive 3D anatomical explorer, alert-management workflows, mission routines, and a NASA-linked science library. It keeps simulated telemetry separate from manually entered demonstration records.

By combining individual health-awareness tools with a mission-level overview, AstroVitals PAK demonstrates a potential approach to making crew-health information more accessible and understandable. The prototype is educational and demonstrative; it is not a medical device or a clinically validated monitoring system.
details:
AstroVitals PAK is a browser-based astronaut health-monitoring prototype designed around the challenges of long-duration human spaceflight. It provides two complementary perspectives: a mission-level overview for monitoring synthetic crew profiles and individual workflows for recording and reviewing health-related information.

The application includes Mission Control for four synthetic crew members, manual health check-ins, simulated telemetry, historical analytics, personal-baseline comparisons, anomaly and alert workflows, mission routines, and an interactive 3D anatomical explorer. Users can rotate and zoom the anatomical model, switch anatomical views, select body regions, and review contextual information. A NASA Science Library connects selected monitoring topics with publicly available NASA human-spaceflight research references.

The system was developed using React, JavaScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, Recharts, and browser localStorage. It is deployed through Netlify, with its source code maintained in a public GitHub repository.

The project's creative contribution is its integration of crew self-assessment, anatomical exploration, descriptive health analytics, and mission-level awareness in one interactive interface. The design emphasizes usability, clear separation of simulated and manually entered data, scientific traceability, and explicit limitations.

All crew profiles and automated telemetry are synthetic. The application is a demonstration prototype, not a medical device, operational spacecraft system, or clinically validated decision-support tool.
